rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its "Figma puts a $25 price on the handoff between designers and front-end engineers" turns an actual disclosed pricing change into a beat-shaped story with the exact missing proof, while B's "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" invents a competitive battlefield the update did not give it. B has usable bones, but it keeps reaching for drama and then asking proof questions to launder the reach.
gaps_in_A: "The launch is the first substantive product move framed against the collapsed Adobe acquisition" overstates the supplied facts. The update says the launch follows the Adobe deal collapse; it does not say first, substantive, or framed that way by Figma.
"Design-to-code has been promised for a decade" may be useful context, but it is not in the update. Source it or cut it.

"If a tool already inside most Fortune 500 companies starts emitting code that ships to production" leans past "working front-end code." A catches the proof problem, but the angle headline still risks implying production use before a customer says so.
gaps_in_B: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" is the big foul. The update gives design-to-code and prompt-to-layout, not prompt-to-app competition with every AI coding tool.
"dominated by smaller AI-native code-generation startups" is invented market framing. No competitors or market structure were supplied.
"The Adobe deal died. Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet" stacks unsupported drama on top of a real sequence. No fact says this was an answer or Figma's biggest bet.

"automating a specific, common junior task" smuggles in a labor-impact claim the update does not support. The proof section admits the data is missing, which is not a license to pitch the angle anyway.
